hook.situation: You want to tell a Korean friend 'I drink coffee every morning.' You know the word 커피, you know 마셔요 — but you're not sure what goes between them. Is it 커피가? 커피는? 커피를? One small particle changes the entire grammatical logic of the sentence.
objectives: Attach 을 or 를 correctly after the object in any present-tense sentence
Say what you eat, drink, study, read, and write every day
Use the short negative (안) to say what you don't do
hook.whyItMatters: 을/를 is the particle that tells listeners WHAT is being acted on. Without it your sentences sound like a list of disconnected words. Once this clicks, you can build an unlimited number of complete action sentences — and Koreans will immediately know you understand Korean sentence structure.

grammarNotes.title: 을/를 — The Object Marker
grammarNotes.mentalModel: Think of 을/를 as an ARROW pointing from the verb back to what it hits. '밥을 먹어요' — the arrow from 먹어요 points back through 을 to 밥. Whatever the action hits, receives, or affects gets the 을/를 arrow. If there's no arrow, listeners don't know what's being eaten/studied/drunk.
grammarNotes.formation: Noun ending in a consonant + 을 / Noun ending in a vowel + 를

examples.note: 밥 ends in consonant ㅂ → 을 is attached; the arrow points from 먹어요 to 밥
커피 ends in vowel 이 → 를 is attached; 마시다 (to drink) hits 커피
한국어 ends in vowel 어 → 를; the studying action is directed at Korean
책 ends in consonant ㄱ → 을; reading is directed at the book
음악 ends in consonant ㄱ → 을; listening is directed at the music

a.en: I drink coffee. (coffee is the object being drunk)

b.en: There is coffee. / I have coffee. (coffee is the subject that exists)

contrastPairs.explanation: Same word 커피, completely different particles. 를 = coffee is what gets drunk (object). 가 = coffee is the thing that exists (subject). The particle tells you the coffee's role in the sentence.

b.en: Music is good. / I like music.

contrastPairs.explanation: 을 marks music as the object being listened to — an active directed action. 이 marks music as the subject of a description. Korean 좋다 (to be good/likeable) takes a subject, not an object — so you can't say 음악을 좋아요 here.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English verbs like 'study' don't need a special particle before their object — you just say 'I study Korean.' Korean does require 을/를. Dropping it sounds like you're just naming things ('I ... Korean ... study') rather than building a proper sentence. Beginners drop 을/를 most often with study, eat, and drink because those sentences feel 'obvious' — but the particle is still required for natural Korean.

exceptions: In fast casual speech, Koreans often drop 을/를 when the object is obvious: 뭐 먹어요? is more natural than the full 뭐를 먹어요? Learn the full frame first, then notice when native speakers shorten it.
하다 verbs like 공부하다, 운동하다 can be split into noun + 를 + 하다: 공부를 해요 = 공부해요 — both are correct
뭐 (what) is usually used without 를 in everyday questions: 뭐 먹어요? is the natural spoken form.

grammarNotes.title: 안 V — The Short Negative (I don't / I'm not doing)
grammarNotes.mentalModel: Think of 안 as a STOP SIGN placed right in front of the verb. You're driving toward the action, and 안 stops it before it happens. 먹어요 = eating happens. 안 먹어요 = the stop sign blocks the eating. The sentence structure is identical — you just insert the stop sign.
grammarNotes.formation: 안 + Verb-아요/어요/해요 (for pure verbs) / Noun + 안 + 해요 (for noun+하다 verbs)

examples.en: I don't eat. / I'm not eating.
examples.note: Stop sign 안 placed directly before 먹어요 — the simplest pattern
안 blocks 마시다; works with any drink or alcohol context
With noun+하다 verbs: split the noun (공부) away and put 안 between noun and 해요 — NOT 안 공부해요
Same noun+하다 split rule: 운동 + 안 + 해요; 안 goes between the noun and 해요
안 in front of the verb stem; same stop-sign pattern

a.en: I don't eat it. (simple everyday negative)

b.en: I do not eat it. (more deliberate / slightly formal)

contrastPairs.explanation: Both mean the same thing, but 안 V feels like a quick natural statement (stop-sign dropped in), while V지 않아요 sounds more considered and is common in writing. In daily speech, 안 V is far more frequent.
With noun+하다 verbs, the 안 MUST split the noun from 해요. Saying 안 공부해요 sounds unnatural to Korean ears. The rule: whenever the verb is [noun]+하다, split it: [noun] + 안 + 해요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English puts the negative before the whole verb phrase: 'I don't study.' Korean with noun+하다 verbs splits the compound: the noun comes first, then 안, then 해요. English speakers try to put 안 at the very front (mirroring 'don't'), but with noun+하다 verbs this sounds wrong. Pure verbs like 먹다, 마시다 can take 안 directly before them — but compound verbs need the split.

exceptions: 못 (cannot) is different from 안 (don't/won't): 안 먹어요 = I don't eat it (choice) / 못 먹어요 = I can't eat it (inability or restriction)
With 있다/없다, don't use 안: use 없어요 instead of 안 있어요 for 'there isn't'
모르다 (to not know) is its own negative — don't say 안 알아요 to mean 'I don't know'; say 몰라요

exampleSentence.note: 점심 ends in consonant ㅁ → 을; eating is directed at lunch
물 ends in consonant ㄹ → 을; the drinking action hits 물
한국어 ends in vowel 어 → 를; can also split: 한국어 공부를 해요
책 ends in consonant ㄱ → 을; reading is directed at the book
일기 ends in vowel 기 → 를; writing is directed at the diary
음악 ends in consonant ㄱ → 을; listening is directed at the music
영화 ends in vowel 아 → 를; watching is directed at the movie
운동하다 has no object here — not everything needs 을/를; negative form: 운동 안 해요
Noun+하다 split negative: 일 + 안 + 해요 — the stop sign goes between noun and verb

exampleSentence.en: Are you eating? / Do you eat rice?
exampleSentence.note: 밥 ends in consonant ㅂ → 을; 밥을 먹다 is the most common eating phrase in Korean
커피 ends in vowel 이 → 를; 마시다 is directed at the drink.

exampleSentence.en: I drink a lot of water.
exampleSentence.note: 물 ends in consonant ㄹ → 을; 많이 = a lot, modifying the verb
책 ends in consonant ㄱ → 을; reading is directed at the book.
음악 ends in consonant ㄱ → 을; listening is directed at the music.
영화 ends in vowel 아 → 를; watching is directed at the movie.
매일 is a time adverb — it doesn't need a particle; it modifies the entire sentence

exampleSentence.en: I drink a lot of water.
exampleSentence.note: 많이 (adverb) modifies the verb directly — no particle needed on the adverb itself

extendedDialogue.setting: Jihee (지희) and her coworker Minho (민호) are chatting over lunch about their daily habits

lines.speaker: 지희
lines.en: Minho, do you eat breakfast every day?
lines.grammarNote: 아침을 먹어요 — 아침 ends in consonant ㅁ → 을; eating (먹다) is directed at breakfast

lines.speaker: 민호
lines.en: No, I don't eat breakfast. I'm busy.
lines.grammarNote: 아침을 안 먹어요 — the stop-sign 안 goes directly before 먹어요 (a pure verb, not noun+하다)

lines.speaker: 지희
lines.ko: 그래요? 저는 매일 밥을 먹어요. 물을 많이 마셔요.
lines.romanization: Geuraeyo? Jeoneun maeil babeul meogeoyo. Mureul mani masyeoyo.
lines.en: Really? I eat rice every day. I drink a lot of water.
lines.grammarNote: 밥을 먹어요 and 물을 마셔요 both use 을 because 밥 and 물 end in consonants. 많이 modifies 마셔요; it does not take a particle.

lines.speaker: 민호
lines.en: I drink coffee. That's my breakfast.
lines.grammarNote: 커피를 마셔요 — 커피 ends in vowel 이 → 를 attaches; drinking is directed at coffee

lines.speaker: 지희
lines.grammarNote: 한국어를 공부해요 — 한국어 ends in vowel 어 → 를; this is also valid as 한국어 공부를 해요 (split form)

lines.speaker: 민호
lines.ko: 네, 매일 한국어를 공부해요. 그런데 책을 안 읽어요.
lines.romanization: Ne, maeil hangugeoreul gongbuhaeyo. Geureonde chaegeul an ilgeoyo.
lines.en: Yes, I study Korean every day. But I don't read books.
lines.grammarNote: 한국어를 공부해요 uses 를 because 한국어 ends in a vowel. 책을 안 읽어요 keeps 을 on the object and puts 안 before the pure verb 읽어요.

lines.speaker: 지희
lines.ko: 저는 책을 읽어요. 그리고 음악을 들어요.
lines.romanization: Jeoneun chaegeul ilgeoyo. Geurigo eumageul deureoyo.
lines.en: I read books. And I listen to music.
lines.grammarNote: 책을 읽어요 and 음악을 들어요 both use 을 because 책 and 음악 end in consonants. Two clean object sentences.

lines.speaker: 민호
lines.ko: 좋아요. 오늘은 영화를 안 봐요. 책을 읽어요.
lines.romanization: Joayo. Oneureun yeonghwareul an bwayo. Chaegeul ilgeoyo.
lines.en: Good. Today I won't watch a movie. I'll read a book.
lines.grammarNote: 영화를 안 봐요 puts 안 before the pure verb 봐요. 책을 읽어요 keeps 을 because 책 ends in consonant ㄱ.

readingText.title: 수빈의 하루 일과 (Subin's Daily Routine)
readingText.body: 저는 매일 아침 밥을 먹어요. 커피를 마셔요. 회사에서 이메일을 써요. 보고서를 읽어요. 점심에는 동료들과 밥을 먹어요. 퇴근 후에는 음악을 들어요. 한국어를 공부해요. 드라마를 봐요. 주말에는 운동 안 해요. 그냥 책을 읽어요.
readingText.bodyTranslation: Every morning I eat a meal. I drink coffee. At work I write emails. I read reports. At lunch I eat with my coworkers. After work I listen to music. I study Korean. I watch dramas. On weekends I don't exercise. I just read books.

comprehensionQuestions.question: What two things does Subin do in the morning?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 밥을 먹어요 (eats a meal) and 커피를 마셔요 (drinks coffee).

comprehensionQuestions.question: What two things does Subin do after work?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 음악을 들어요 (listens to music) and 한국어를 공부해요 (studies Korean)

comprehensionQuestions.question: Find all the 을/를 in the text. For each one, explain why 을 or 를 is used — not the other form.
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 밥을 (ㅂ consonant ending → 을), 커피를 (이 vowel ending → 를), 이메일을 (ㄹ consonant ending → 을), 보고서를 (어 vowel ending → 를), 밥을 (again, ㅂ → 을), 음악을 (ㄱ consonant ending → 을), 한국어를 (어 vowel ending → 를), 드라마를 (아 vowel ending → 를), 책을 (ㄱ consonant ending → 을). The rule: consonant-ending nouns take 을, vowel-ending nouns take 를.

culturalNote.title: 밥 먹었어요? — The Korean greeting that's really about food
culturalNote.body: In Korea, one of the most common informal greetings is '밥 먹었어요?' (Have you eaten?) — said instead of 'How are you?' to close friends and family. Offering food is central to Korean social bonding. Answering 'yes' (네, 먹었어요) or 'not yet' (아직요) is totally normal. Notice that in this casual greeting, the particle 을 is often dropped: '밥 먹었어요?' rather than '밥을 먹었어요?' This is the natural particle-dropping that Koreans do in fast speech — but you now know the full form with 을, which makes the shortened form easy to understand.

inlineExercises.explanation: 아침 ends in consonant ㅁ, so it takes 을. 를 is only used after vowel-ending nouns. 이 and 가 are subject markers, not object markers — they mark who is doing the action, not what receives it.

커피 ends in vowel 이, so it takes 를. 을 is for consonant-ending nouns. 은/는 are topic markers, not object markers — they set the topic of the sentence, which is different from marking what is being drunk.

inlineExercises.prompt: 다음 문장을 자연스럽게 고쳐보세요: '저는 안 공부해요.'
inlineExercises.explanation: 공부하다 is a noun+하다 verb. In the everyday short negative, split it into 공부 + 안 + 해요. Pure verbs take 안 right before the verb (안 먹어요), but noun+하다 verbs usually split: 공부 안 해요, 운동 안 해요, 일 안 해요.
한국어 ends in vowel 어, so it takes 를. This is one of the most common sentences a Korean learner will ever say — 한국어를 공부해요 — so it's worth drilling until it's automatic.

inlineExercises.hint: 영화 ends in a vowel — which form of the object marker do you need? And 보다 is a pure verb, so where does 안 go?

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence correctly says 'I don't study' using the 안 negative?
inlineExercises.explanation: 공부 안 해요 is correct — noun + stop-sign + 해요. '안 공부해요' is wrong because 안 can't go before a noun-verb compound. '공부를 않아요' is missing the -지 needed for the long negative form (공부를 하지 않아요). '안 공부를 해요' mixes up the word order in an unnatural way.

inlineExercises.prompt: Your friend says '책을 읽어요.' What is the role of 을 in this sentence?
options: It marks 책 as the subject doing the reading.
It marks 책 as the object receiving the action of reading.
It marks 책 as a topic being discussed.
It is a verb ending attached to 책.
inlineExercises.correct: It marks 책 as the object receiving the action of reading.
inlineExercises.explanation: 을/를 is the object marker — it marks WHAT gets acted upon. 책 is what is being read. Subject markers (이/가) mark who does the action; topic markers (은/는) set what we're talking about. 을/를 is specifically for the thing that receives the verb's action.

bullets: 을/를 = ARROW from verb to object: consonant-ending noun + 을 / vowel-ending noun + 를
안 = STOP SIGN before a pure verb (안 먹어요); for noun+하다 verbs split it: noun + 안 + 해요
Key daily verbs with their objects: 밥을 먹다, 커피를 마시다, 한국어를 공부하다, 책을 읽다, 음악을 듣다, 영화를 보다
summaryCard.nextChapterTeaser: Next: Chapter 6 introduces 에 and 에서 — the location particles that tell Koreans WHERE you go, WHERE you are, and WHERE actions happen. Combined with 을/를 from this chapter, you'll build full sentences like '도서관에서 한국어를 공부해요.'
